Toasting and [[Sound system (Jamaican)|soundsystem]] cultures were also influential in genres outside of hip-hop that still included [[rapping]] – such as [[Grime (music genre)|grime]], [[Jungle music|jungle]], and [[UK garage]].{{Cite news|last=Beaumont-Thomas|first=Ben|url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2018/jun/01/inside-grime-true-history-dan-hancox-dj-target-wiley-dizzee-rascal-stormzy|title='You can't escape its inspiration': inside the true history of grime|date=1 June 2018|work=The Guardian|access-date=11 February 2020|issn=0261-3077|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181018161811/https://www.theguardian.com/music/2018/jun/01/inside-grime-true-history-dan-hancox-dj-target-wiley-dizzee-rascal-stormzy|archive-date=18 October 2018|url-status=live}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.factmag.com/2016/07/06/roots-and-future-documentary-black-british-music-jungle-garage-grime-dubstep/|title=Hear a documentary on black British music from jungle to dubstep|date=6 July 2016|website=FACT Magazine|access-date=11 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191108224525/https://www.factmag.com/2016/07/06/roots-and-future-documentary-black-british-music-jungle-garage-grime-dubstep/|archive-date=8 November 2019|url-status=live}} In 2003, ''[[The Times]]'' described British hip-hop's broad-ranging approach:
..."UK hip-hop" is a broad sonic church, encompassing anything made in Britain by musicians informed or inspired by hip-hop's possibilities, whose music is a response to the same stimuli that gave birth to rap in New York in the mid-Seventies.
Although the underground scene was well established by the late 1980s, UK rap music saw little commercial success for several decades. Outside of a few exceptions such as [[Derek B]] and later the birth of [[Trip hop|trip-hop]], from the 1980s until the early 2010s UK rap made up a small percentage of album sales in the domestic market.{{Cite web |title=UK stars including Central Cee, Dave and Digga D help Rap claim record share of albums market |url=https://www.musicweek.com/talent/read/uk-stars-including-central-cee-dave-and-digga-d-help-rap-claim-record-share-of-albums-market/087721 |access-date=26 October 2024 |website=www.musicweek.com |language=en}}{{Cite web |date=19 July 2023 |title=The History of British Hip Hop |url=https://www.icmp.ac.uk/blog/history-british-hip-hop |access-date=26 October 2024 |website=ICMP |language=en}} Performers saw wider success in the 2020s, including [[Stormzy]] headlining [[Glastonbury Festival]], [[Dave (rapper)|Dave]] releasing back-to-back UK number one albums with ''[[Psychodrama (album)|Psychodrama]]'' followed by ''[[We're All Alone in This Together]]'', and [[Little Simz]] winning the [[Mercury Prize]].{{Cite web |title=Britain's rap revolution |url=https://crackmagazine.net/article/what-just-happened/britains-rap-revolution/ |access-date=26 October 2024 |website=Crack Magazine}} == History == === Origins === As in the US, British hip-hop emerged as a scene from [[graffiti]] and [[breakdancing]], and then through to DJing and [[rapping]] live at parties and club nights, with its supporters predominantly listening to and influenced by US hip-hop. Unlike in the US, the British hip-hop scene was cross-racial from the beginning, as diverse [[ethnic group]]s in Britain tend not to live in [[Racial segregation|segregated]] areas, even in areas with a high percentage of non-white individuals. Such places allow youth to share culture with one another, including musical genres such as hip-hop.{{cite news |title="Urban Breakbeat Culture: Repercussions of Hip-Hop in the United Kingdom", pp. 86–101 in Global Noise: Rap and Hip Hop Outside of the USA, edited by Tony Mitchell. Middletown, CT: Wesleyan University Press.|first=David|last=Hesmondhalgh}} Cross pollination through migrating [[West Indies|West Indians]] helped develop a community interested in the music. The integration of [[Sound system (Jamaican)|sound systems]] represent a distinct [[British Caribbean]] influence. Sound systems allowed for powerful syncopated bass runs and the ability to bring this sound to other venues creating a [[club culture]].Hesmondhalgh, DJ and Melville, C (2002) Urban Breakbeat Culture – Repercussions of Hip-Hop in the United Kingdom. In: Global Noise: Rap and Hip Hop Outside the USA. Wesleyan University Press. There were, however, British tunes starting to appear. There are an abundance of records that are often credited with being the first British hip-hop release, "Christmas Rapping" by Dizzy Heights (Polydor, 1982), is often credited as such, as well as the slightly later released "London Bridge" by [[Newtrament]] (Jive Records, 1983).{{cite web|url=http://www.low-life.fsnet.co.uk/ukhiphop/story/early_doors.htm |title=Low Life/British hip hop, UK hip hop: the story find |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061010071345/http://www.low-life.fsnet.co.uk/ukhiphop/story/early_doors.htm |archive-date=10 October 2006 |url-status=dead}} Dizzy Heights was the first MC to be signed to a major label.{{Cite web|date=1 November 2020|title=Ty and the history of UK hip-hop – Features – Mixmag|url=https://mixmag.net/feature/ty-and-the-history-of-uk-rap|access-date=23 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201101150514/https://mixmag.net/feature/ty-and-the-history-of-uk-rap|archive-date=1 November 2020}} Two singles from 1980 precede both of these however, namely Allen & Blewitt's novelty record "Chip Shop Wrapping", released in 1980, a parody of [[The Sugarhill Gang]]'s "[[Rapper's Delight]]", and Bo Kool's "Money (No Love)". The instrumental for "Money (No Love)" was produced by [[Funk Masters]] member Tony Williams, and would turn out to be an influential release in its own right, going on to inspire DJ's from New York to employ influences from [[dub music]].{{Cite web|title=Looking back on 40 years since the first rap hit on the UK chart|url=https://www.officialcharts.com/chart-news/looking-back-on-40-years-since-the-first-rap-hit-sugarhill-gang-s-rapper-s-delight__27830/|access-date=19 December 2020|website=www.officialcharts.com|language=en}}{{Cite web|date=26 April 2016|title=GREG WILSON'S DISCOTHEQUE ARCHIVES #1|url=https://djmag.com/features/greg-wilsons-discotheque-archives|access-date=19 December 2020|website=DJMag.com|archive-date=6 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201206132412/https://djmag.com/features/greg-wilsons-discotheque-archives|url-status=dead}} In Scotland, actor and stand-up comedian [[Johnny Beattie]] released "The Glasgow Rap" in 1983, receiving some chart success at the time. He later claimed to be "Scotland's first rap star".{{Cite web|title=Obituary: Johnny Beattie|url=https://www.thestage.co.uk/obituaries--archive/obituaries/johnny-beattie|access-date=23 December 2020|website=The Stage|language=En}}{{Cite news|date=12 December 2012|title=Johnny Beattie: 60 years In The Limelight|language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-scotland-20677255|access-date=23 December 2020}} This was one of several British [[Novelty song|novelty]] or [[comedy hip-hop]] singles which hit the UK charts during the 1980s, including "Wikka Wrap" by [[the Evasions]], "Snot Rap" by [[Kenny Everett]], "[['Ullo John! Gotta New Motor?]]" by [[Alexei Sayle]], "Rat Rappin'" by [[Roland Rat]], and later in the decade, "[[Stutter Rap (No Sleep til Bedtime)]]" by [[Morris Minor and the Majors]] and "[[Loadsamoney]]" by [[Harry Enfield]].{{cite web |last=Thomas |first=Darin |date=11 December 2019 |title=20 bizarre novelty songs from the 80s you've probably never heard of |url=https://metro.co.uk/2016/07/01/20-bizarre-novelty-songs-from-the-80s-youve-probably-never-heard-of-5973831/ |website=[[metro.co.uk]] |access-date=29 January 2025}} There were also early pop records which dabbled with rap – such as [[Adam and the Ants]]' "[[Ant Rap]]" (CBS, 1981) and [[Wham!]]'s "[[Wham Rap! (Enjoy What You Do)]]" (Inner Vision, 1982) — but these are often considered pop appropriations of US rap.{{cite book|last1=Ogg|first1=Alex|title=Paid in full? an introduction to brit-hop, grime and 2020|url-status=live}} Even earlier than this, in 1979, [[Ian Dury and the Blockheads]] released "[[Reasons to Be Cheerful, Part 3|Reasons to Be Cheerful (Part 3)]]", another record with influences from hip-hop.{{Cite web|title=Ian Dury – Rockabilly Central|url=http://www.rockabilly.net/articles/iandury3.shtml|access-date=19 December 2020|website=www.rockabilly.net}} Then [[Sex Pistols]] manager [[Malcolm McLaren]]'s "[[Buffalo Gals (Malcolm McLaren song)|Buffalo Gals]]" (Charisma, 1982), featuring the New York hip-hop group [[World's Famous Supreme Team]], was the breakthrough hit that introduced the genre to the United Kingdom{{Cite web|url=http://old.manchesterconfidential.co.uk/Entertainment-and-Sport/Music/HomeGrown-the-story-of-UK-hip-hop|title=HomeGrown: the story of UK hip-hop|website=Manchester Confidential|access-date=11 February 2020}} — McLaren's ''[[Duck Rock]]'' album as a whole experimented with many musical styles from around the world. "Buffalo Gals" and another track from the album, "World's Famous" which also featured the group, used techniques which have been established in hip-hop in the United States, such as [[sampling (music)|sampling]] and [[scratching]]. McLaren even included a song referencing the '[[Double Dutch (jump rope)|Double Dutch]]' dance that was popular among breakdancing crews in New York at the time.{{Cite web|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/double-dutchs-forgotten-hip-hop-origins-456/|title=Double Dutch's Forgotten Hip-Hop Origins|last=Schwartzberg|first=Lauren|date=31 March 2015|website=Vice|access-date=11 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191001205746/https://www.vice.com/en_au/article/nn974m/double-dutchs-forgotten-hip-hop-origins-456|archive-date=1 October 2019|url-status=live}} Over the next few years, more UK hip-hop and [[electro music]] was released: ''Street Sounds Electro UK'' (Street Sounds, 1984), which was produced by [[Greg Wilson (DJ)|Greg Wilson]] and featured an early appearance from MC Kermit, who later went on to form the Wilson produced [[Ruthless Rap Assassins]]; [[Mastermind Herbie|the Rapologists]]' "Kids Rap/Party Rap" (Billy Boy, 1984) and Grandmaster Richie Rich's "Don't Be Flash" (Spin Offs, 1985).{{cite web |title=The 10 records that helped British hip-hop find its own voice |url=https://thevinylfactory.com/features/the-10-records-that-helped-british-hip-hop-find-its-own-voice/ |website=[[The Vinyl Factory]] |access-date=24 June 2018 |date=17 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180624150550/https://thevinylfactory.com/features/the-10-records-that-helped-british-hip-hop-find-its-own-voice/ |archive-date=24 June 2018 |url-status=live }} Releases were still few and far between, and the scene remained predominantly underground.[[File:Tim Westwood 2012.jpg|thumb|right|Westwood's official YouTube channel, Tim Westwood TV, has currently over 617 million video views and over 1.41 million subscribers. The channel has videos of freestyles and interviews from some of the most successful hip-hop artists, including [[Notorious B.I.G.]], [[Eminem]], [[Jay-Z]], [[Nas]] and [[Lil Wayne]].]] Although record labels began to take note of the [[underground scene]] throughout the 1980s and 1990s, radio play and publicity were still a difficulty in helping the fledgling scene to grow, and the scene only managed to survive through word of mouth and the patronage of [[pirate radio]] stations around the country. Mainstream radio did play British hip-hop on occasion, supported by such well-known DJs as [[Dave Pearce]], [[Tim Westwood]], Steve Barker{{citation needed|date=March 2021}} and [[John Peel]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.mtv.com/news/1493022/john-peel-legendary-dj-and-champion-of-acts-from-bowie-to-franz-ferdinand-dies/|title=John Peel, Legendary DJ And Champion of Acts From Bowie To Franz Ferdinand, Dies|last=Montgomery|first=James|publisher=MTV News|access-date=11 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190526151054/http://www.mtv.com/news/1493022/john-peel-legendary-dj-and-champion-of-acts-from-bowie-to-franz-ferdinand-dies/|archive-date=26 May 2019|url-status=dead}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.mixcloud.com/colinmillar/old-school-uk-hip-hop-radio-sessions-volume-5/|title=Mixcloud|website=Mixcloud|access-date=11 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111224014909/http://www.mixcloud.com/colinmillar/old-school-uk-hip-hop-radio-sessions-volume-5/|archive-date=24 December 2011|url-status=live}} A significant development in early UK rap was the nationwide Def Jam '87 Tour, which featured [[LL Cool J]] (billed as the headliner), [[Eric B. & Rakim]], and a then-emerging [[Public Enemy (band)|Public Enemy]]. In an interview for ''What Do You Call It? From Grassroots to the Golden Era of UK Rap'' (2024), DJ, photographer, and broadcaster [[Normski]] described the experience to David Kane: "You've never heard anything so loud. We heard the records, but we've never seen it with so much ferocity in the flesh. By the end of the night, everyone was so pumped. That would have inspired everyone to go and do something badass."{{Cite book |last=Kane |first=David |title=What Do You Call It? From Grassroots to the Golden Era of UK Rap |publisher=Velocity Press |year=2024 |isbn=978-1-913231-61-3 |url=https://velocitypress.uk/product/what-do-you-call-it-book/}} British hip-hop in the 1980s was not just confined to music and break-dancing, but also involved the spread of New York City-style graffiti – another [[hip-hop|integral element of US hip hop culture]] — to London and other UK inner-city areas, both on walls and trains. The most direct influence was, however, on graffiti painted in [[London Underground]] trains. Teenagers from inner London and other European cities who were into electro-hip-hop and had family and other links to New York City had by the mid-1980s taken up some of the traditions of subway graffiti and exported them home, although legendary New York writers like Brim, Bio, and Futura had themselves played a significant role in establishing such links when they visited London in the early-to-mid-1980s and 'put up pieces' on or near the west London end of the [[Metropolitan Line]]. Almost as significantly, just when [[subway graffiti]] was on the decline in New York City, some British teenagers who had spent time with family in Queens and the Bronx returned to London with a "mission" to Americanise the London Underground through painting New York City-style graffiti on trains. These small groups of London 'train writers' adopted many of the styles and lifestyles of their New York City forebears, painting graffiti train pieces and in general 'bombing' the system, but favouring only a few selected underground lines seen as most suitable for train graffiti. Although on a substantially smaller scale than what had existed in New York City, graffiti on London Underground trains became seen as enough of a problem by the mid-1980s to provoke the British Transport Police to establish its own graffiti squad modelled directly on and in consultation with that of the New York City MTA. At the same time, graffiti art on London Underground trains generated some interest in the media and arts, leading to several art galleries putting on exhibitions of some of the art work (on canvas) of a few London train writers as well as TV documentaries on London hip-hop culture like the BBC's ''Bad Meaning Good'', which included a section featuring interviews with London train writers and a few examples of their pieces. While many early rappers from the UK, such as [[Derek B]], imitated the styles and accents of their US heroes, there were many who realised that to merely transpose US forms would rob UK hip-hop of the ability to speak for a [[disenfranchised]] British [[constituency]] in the way that US hip-hop so successfully spoke to, and for, its audience. Attempts were made by UK rappers to develop styles more obviously rooted in British [[semantics]], [[syntax]] and [[dialectical]] [[linguistic]] praxis and practices — [[Rodney P]] of the [[London Posse]] deliberately chose a London accent{{what|date=June 2025}} – although many succeeded only in adopting a slurred hybrid that located the rap "somewhere in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean".Hesmondhalgh, David and Caspar Melville. "Urban Breakbeat Culture: Repercussions of Hip-Hop in the United Kingdom." In Global Noise: Rap and Hip-Hop Outside the USA, 86–110. Middletown: Wesleyan University Press, 2001. ===Development: Late 1980s–early 1990s=== The first record label devoted to releasing UK hip-hop acts was founded in 1986. [[Simon Harris (musician)|Simon Harris]]' [[Music of Life]] label was home to rapper [[Derek B]], the first UK rapper to achieve chart success. He even collaborated with [[Public Enemy (band)|Public Enemy]] on his album ''[[Bullet from a Gun (album)|Bullet from a Gun]]''{{Cite web|url=http://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/derek-b-rapper-and-producer-who-became-the-first-uk-hip-hop-artist-to-infiltrate-the-british-pop-1864852.html|title=Derek B: Rapper and producer who became the first UK hip-hop artist to|date=12 January 2010|website=The Independent|access-date=11 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180106090734/http://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/derek-b-rapper-and-producer-who-became-the-first-uk-hip-hop-artist-to-infiltrate-the-british-pop-1864852.html|archive-date=6 January 2018|url-status=live}} and was the first British rapper to appear on ''[[Top of the Pops]]''.{{Cite news|last=Michaels|first=Sean|url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2009/nov/17/british-rapper-derek-b-dies|title=British rapper Derek B dies at 44|date=17 November 2009|work=The Guardian|access-date=11 February 2020|issn=0261-3077|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190228130415/https://www.theguardian.com/music/2009/nov/17/british-rapper-derek-b-dies|archive-date=28 February 2019|url-status=live}} Building on Derek B's success, [[Music of Life]] went on to sign groups such as [[Hijack (group)|Hijack]], the [[Demon Boyz]], [[Hardnoise]] (later Son of Noise) and [[MC Duke]]. Their ''Hard as Hell'' series mixed homegrown talent like Thrashpack and the [[She Rockers]] with US artists such as [[Professor Griff]]. Music of Life was swiftly followed by other labels such as [[Mango Records]] and Kold Sweat. Another successful British hip-hop artist that emerged from Music of Life was [[Asher D (Jamaican-British rapper)|Asher D]], whose Jamaican origins showed through in his vocal style. In 1988, in collaboration with [[Daddy Freddy]], Asher D released one of the first hip-hop [[dancehall]] fusion albums, ''[[Ragamuffin Hip-Hop]]''.{{Cite web |title=Ty and the history of UK rap |url=https://mixmag.net/feature/ty-and-the-history-of-uk-rap |access-date=19 June 2023 |website=Mixmag}} [[File:Slick Rick - The Ruler.jpg|thumb|259x259px|Slick Rick is an English rapper.]] Moving away from its US roots, British hip-hop started to develop its own sounds: acts like [[Hijack (group)|Hijack]], II Tone Committee, Eastborm, Killa Instinct, [[Hardnoise]], and [[Silver Bullet (rapper)|Silver Bullet]] developed a fast and [[hardcore hip-hop|hardcore]] style (often referred to as Britcore), while many other acts took influences from elsewhere. Britcore acts were amongst the first to receive wide-spread attention across [[continental Europe]]. [[Caveman (group)|Caveman]] and [[Outlaw Posse]] developed a jazz influenced style, whilst MC Mell'O' mixed [[jazz]] and hardcore. [[London Posse]], [[Black Radical Mk II]] and DJ Ruf Cut And Tuf C were more influenced by [[reggae]] and [[disco]] whilst the [[Wee Papa Girl Rappers]], [[Cookie Crew]] and [[Monie Love]] achieved chart success with more radio-friendly hip-hop. However, despite the chart success of some British-born hip-hop artists – for example [[Monie Love]], [[Slick Rick]], [[Young MC]] and [[MF Doom]], who all moved to the US – the majority of the scene was still underground and small scale. Kinetic Effect joined the scene in the early 1980s and was part of rap outfit 2 the Top as D-Koy; later, in 1991, he teamed with Insane Macbeth to record "Borderin' Insanity" (released in 1993) and in 1995, he recorded "Man Bites Dog"/"The Effect of Fear"[http://www.heroesofukhiphop.com/Kinetic.htm] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120204163244/http://www.heroesofukhiphop.com/Kinetic.htm|date=4 February 2012}} Their song "The Rhythm I Give 'Em" made the UK Top 10 Hip-hop chart. In 1987, [[Positive Beat Records]]{{cite web |url=http://www.discogs.com/label/Positive+Beat+Records |title=Positive Beat Records – CDs and Vinyl at Discogs |publisher=discogs |access-date=24 February 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081028213606/http://www.discogs.com/label/Positive+Beat+Records |archive-date=28 October 2008 |url-status=live }} came out of the hotbed of early UK hip-hop, [[Ladbroke Grove]] in London with two releases. The label followed up the single "It's Getting Rough" by Rocky X and D-D Dance{{cite web |url=http://top80.pl/disc/release/1338179/RockyX/(It%27s+Getting)+Ruff |title=Italo Disco, Euro Disco, Muzyka, Ludzie, Radio, Forum, Klimat, Czat |publisher=TOP80.PL |access-date=24 February 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090430073902/http://top80.pl/disc/release/1338179/RockyX/(It%27s+Getting)+Ruff |archive-date=30 April 2009 |url-status=live }} with the Various Artists' ''Known 2 Be Down''[http://www.raphistory.net/database?inc=records&operation=details&ID=3078] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110724025952/http://www.raphistory.net/database?inc=records&operation=details&ID=3078|date=24 July 2011}} album. This featured Sir Drew (of KREW and [[Newtrament]]), MC Flex, [[She Rockers]], Rapski and more of West London's finest rap talents. Other notable labels at the time included [[Liberty Grooves]]Ear to the Ground Magazine, Issue 1 1993 in Tooting, South London. The label itself started in late 1989 with the first release in 1990 by Whirlwind D & Johnny F of [[Solid n Mind]]. Other artists included [[Gutter Snypes]],Rap Trade Magazine, June 1994 Issue 6, Publisher: Pure Impact True Style and [[DJ Noize]]. Liberty Grooves was also a shop and many notable artists such as MC Mell O and [[Braintax]] would perform there. In 1988, Rapski released "The Connection" on 12".{{cite web |url=http://top80.pl/disc/label/Positive+Beat+Records |title=Italo Disco, Euro Disco, Muzyka, Ludzie, Radio, Forum, Klimat, Czat |publisher=TOP80.PL |access-date=2014-02-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090430182155/http://top80.pl/disc/label/Positive+Beat+Records |archive-date=30 April 2009 |url-status=live }} The track was taken from ''Known 2 Be Down'' and was an early example of mixing hip-hop and [[reggae]] in a (London) style. More was to come in the early 1990s in the form of MC Reason (a.k.a. Voice of Reason) with "Symbolise"/"HouseQuake" and Jonie D with "Which Base"/"Ride On" which was performed live on [[ITV (TV network)|ITV]] in 1991. A mindset began to develop – typified by the [[Gunshot (band)|Gunshot]] tune "No Sell Out" (1991), or [[Hardnoise|Son of Noise]]'s "Poor But Hardcore" (1992) — that distrusted successful artists who did not use the hardcore style most associated with the scene. [[Silver Bullet (rapper)|Silver Bullet]]'s chart success was applauded due to an uncompromisingly rapid delivery. As the scene grew, it became less common for British rappers to imitate US accents (those who did were often ridiculed) and British rap became more assured of its identity. ''[[Hip Hop Connection]]'' — the first major British hip-hop magazine – was founded in 1989 and by the early 1990s the British hip-hop scene seemed to be thriving. Not only was there a firm base of rappers in London such as Blade, [[Black Radical Mk II]], Bushkiller (including Sirus) and [[Overlord X]], who cut a [[Discomix]] with [[Jah Shaka]] — but many distinct scenes developed nationally. Jah Shaka recorded a crossover [[dubplate]] [[discomix]] tune with Overlord X (under the moniker Raggafunk ) entitled "Come And Get Me" , which was a retake of a tune from Shaka's [[conscious]] roots "Dub Symphony album" which was eventually released on the Island Records' subsidiary label Mango. Birmingham and the West Midlands gave rise to [[Credit to the Nation]], whose MC Fusion would espouse conscious anti-racist, sexist and homophobic lyrics. The band would also find some brief mainstream success with their [[indie rock]] crossover sound. Leeds spawned [[Braintax]] and Breaking the Illusion (who together founded [[Low Life Records]]) as well as [[Nightmares on Wax]]. Greater Manchester gave birth to the [[Ruthless Rap Assassins]], Krispy 3 (later Krispy), the [[Kaliphz]], [[Jeep Beat Collective]] and [[MC Tunes]]. Bristol's scene has a long history going right back to the early 1980s where links were made with outfits from New York. [[The Fearless Four (group)|The Fearless Four]] came over in 1984 along with graffiti legends the [[Tats Cru]] and [[Rock Steady Crew]]. Bristol (specifically the [[St Pauls, Bristol|St. Pauls]] area) produced The Wild Bunch (later better known as [[Massive Attack]]), and [[Nellee Hooper]] who went on to produce for [[Soul II Soul]], as well as cutting [[dubplate]] [[discomix]]es with [[roots reggae]] artists, [[Horace Andy]] and [[Mad Professor]]. The city later became the home of [[trip hop]] with artists like [[Tricky (musician)|Tricky]] and [[Portishead (band)|Portishead]]. [[Caveman (group)|Caveman]] signed to a major label — [[Profile Records]], the label home of [[Run–D.M.C.]] — and Kold Sweat came into their own, discovering groups like SL Troopers, [[Dynametrix]], Unanimous Decision and Katch 22, whose "Diary of a Blackman" was banned by [[BBC Radio 1|Radio 1]] for using a sound clip from the [[British National Front|National Front]]. In 1991, [[Hijack (group)|Hijack]] released ''The Horns of [[Jericho]]'' (Rhyme Syndicate Records, 1991) on [[Ice-T]]'s recently formed Rhyme Syndicate label. The first single, "The Badman Is Robbin'", was a top 40 hit and they went on sell more than 30,000 albums.{{cite web|url=https://rockthebells.com/articles/hijack-rap-group/|title=HIJACK: THE STORY OF BRITAIN'S "PUBLIC ENEMY"|work=Rock The Bells|author=Philip Mlynar|access-date=4 August 2022|archive-date=4 August 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220804184411/https://rockthebells.com/articles/hijack-rap-group/|url-status=dead}} British hip-hop was affected by the record industry clamping down on [[sampling (music)|sampling]], beginning to charge for the use of samples and prosecuting those who used them without permission. Larger US acts could afford to license samples and still turn a profit for their labels, a luxury not available to many smaller UK artists. One such victim of this was [[Milton Keynes]] group [[the Criminal Minds]]. Their first two releases, the 1990 mini-album ''Guilty as Charged'' and a 1991 EP ''Tales from the Wasteland'' were bogged down by potential sample clearance problems and thus were only ever made available in small numbers. As [[breakbeat hardcore]] music started to become very popular in the UK in the early 1990s, the Criminal Minds turned their attention to making this type of music instead.{{cite web|url=https://internationalorange.io/systems-overload-britcore-and-the-uk/|title=Systems Overload: Britcore and the UK underground|work=International Orange|date=19 November 2020|author=Oli Warwick}} The UK hip-hop boom never achieved its predicted commercial success. Hijack's ''The Horns of Jericho'' was never released in the US, whilst record companies dropped artists, citing poor sales and lack of interest. [[Mango Records]] closed down, and the British public began to turn their affections to [[Jungle music]], a fusion of breakbeat hardcore, dub, [[dancehall]], [[ragga]], hip-hop and [[reggae]], profoundly influenced by the rhythmic dynamics of [[King Tubby]]'s and [[Scientist (musician)|Scientist]] [[discomix]]es and the spatial reverberations of [[Jah Shaka]] and [[Lloyd Coxsone]] sound systems, both of whom attracted followers with an almost religious sense of awe and devotion to sound, specifically, to bass tones and frequencies. Other acts and styles developed from the hip-hop scene, resulting in new genres to describe them – for example [[Massive Attack]]{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/70844.stm |title=BBC News website, Massive Attack on the net |date=29 March 1998 |access-date=2 November 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040509115510/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/sci/tech/70844.stm |archive-date=9 May 2004 |url-status=live }} with [[trip hop]], or [[Galliano (band)|Galliano]], [[Us3]] and [[Urban Species]] with [[acid jazz]]. In the period between 1992 and 1995, the only groups to make much impact were Gunshot and [[The Brotherhood (rap group)|the Brotherhood]]. Gunshot's 1992 album ''Patriot Games'' was a landmark with tracks such as "Mind of a Razor" and "World War 3" becoming British hardcore classics. Formed in the '80s, the Brotherhood released their first record, simply called ''Brotherhood EP'', as a white label in 1991. They went on to release ''Wayz of the Wize'' in 1992, then ''Untitled 93'' and ''XXIII'' in 1993, and ''Hip Hop N' Rap'' in 1994, all on the Bite It! label. None of the records sold in huge numbers but they managed to gain airplay on the [[Tim Westwood]] show and DJ 279's show on [[Choice FM]], gaining them a solid following across the UK. Bite It! also released tracks from artists such as Pauly Ryan and the Scientists of Sound. ===New generation: Late 1990s–early 2000s=== Following an initial flurry of interest from major record labels in the 1980s, by the early 1990s the scene had moved underground after record companies pulled back. In the mid-1990s hip-hop in the UK started to experiment and diversify – often mutating into diverse genres entirely, such as [[trip hop]] and began making inroads into the US market.{{cite web |url=http://www.rocklists.com/q101-1997.html |title=Q101 Top 101 of 1997 |publisher=Rocklists.com |access-date=17 June 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924091722/http://www.rocklists.com/q101-1997.html |archive-date=24 September 2015 |url-status=live }} As the old rappers left the scene, a new generation, raised on hip-hop and [[electronica]], was coming of age: [[The Herbaliser]] released ''Remedies'' ([[Ninja Tune]], 1995), [[Mr. Scruff]] released the "Frolic EP Pt 1" (Pleasure Music, 1995), [[Mark B]] released "Any More Questions?" (Jazz Fudge, 1995) and [[DJ Skitz]] released "Where My Mind Is At/Blessed Be The Manor" (Ronin Records, 1996) featuring a young rapper called [[Roots Manuva]] on guest vocals who had previously released the single "Next Type of Motion" (Sound of Money, 1995). Record labels that attempted to merge British hip-hop style and sensibilities with modern dance music began to emerge, like [[Rae & Christian|Mark Rae]]'s [[Grand Central Records|Grand Central]] (home to Aim, Rae & Christian, and Fingathing, among others) or [[DJ Vadim]]'s Jazz Fudge. Increasingly, these artists managed to avoid the issues surrounding sampling by making music themselves (bands such as the [[Stereo MCs]] began playing instruments and sampling their own tunes) or searching out more obscure records where a most cost effective licensing deal could be arranged. British hip-hop began to go through a renaissance,{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/1482738.stm |title=BBC News website: British hip-hop renaissance |first=Barney |last=Rowntree |date=10 August 2001 |access-date=2 November 2006}} its style shifting from the hardcore template of its youth and moving into more melodic territory. The Brotherhood managed to broker a major deal with Virgin Records in 1995. Continuing their relationship with Trevor Jackson as their producer, they released 3 singles 'Alphabetical Response', 'One Shot', 'Punk Funk' and their album ''[[Elementalz]]'', all in 1996. Their work was met with critical acclaim and they toured solidly with American artists including Cypress Hill, The Roots and WuTang, but big record sales seemed to be very elusive and they parted ways with Virgin in 1998. In late 1996, [[Will Ashon]] started up his new [[Ninja Tune]] backed label [[Big Dada]] and planned a roster of performers. Bandit of Birmingham's MSI/Asylum crew informed Will of [[Juice Aleem]] that he was contemplating who could truly represent the ethos of the new label. Ashon was impressed with the demo and agreed to have Aleem on board. The results of this were the first release of the now famous record label: in 1997 Juice featured on Big Dada record label's first ever release[2], "Misanthropic", under the pseudonym "Alpha Prhyme", a collaboration between himself and [[Luke Vibert]]. In 1998, [[Mark B]] and Blade released "Hitmen for Hire EP", which featured guest appearances from [[Lewis Parker (musician)|Lewis Parker]] and [[Mr Thing]] (of the [[Scratch Perverts]]). The EP was a success, and led to the successful 2001 album ''The Unknown'', which despite never charting in the UK top 75, was still a top 100 success and an even bigger success within its genre. Also, the album spawned the 2001 top 40 single "Ya Don't See the Signs", which was a remix by [[Feeder (band)|Feeder]] frontman [[Grant Nicholas]], after the title track was a top 75 hit and Blade with Mark B supported Feeder. The same year, Bristol's Hombré label released the "2012 EP" from [[Aspects (band)|Aspects]], a benchmark release within the movement. [[Roots Manuva]], [[Blak Twang]], [[Mud Family]], [[Ti2bs]], [[Task Force (band)|Task Force]], [[Phi Life Cypher]], MSI & Asylum, [[Jeep Beat Collective]] and [[Ty (rapper)|Ty]] all came to the public's attention, while veteran acts [[Rodney P]], [[Demon Boyz|Mike J]], and MC Mell'O' returned to the scene. ===Rise to mainstream: 2000s to 2010s=== A new generation of artists emerged following the turn of the century, including [[Jehst]], [[Skinnyman]], [[Nicky Spesh]], [[Foreign Beggars]] and Usmaan. At the same time, a new style of [[electronic music]] emerged in the early 2000s, derivative of [[UK garage]] and [[jungle music|jungle]], with influences from [[dancehall]], [[drum and bass]] and hip-hop; this new genre was dubbed "[[Grime (music)|grime]]" (sometimes called eskibeat or sublow) and effectively superseded UK hip-hop in both popularity and the mainstream conscious. Grime is generally considered to be distinct from hip-hop due to its roots primarily being genres such as UK garage and jungle.{{Cite web|url=https://www.complex.com/pigeons-and-planes/2015/11/grime-hip-hop|title=Deeper Than Rap: Grime is Not a Subgenre of Hip-Hop|website=Complex|access-date=14 September 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190914112019/https://www.complex.com/pigeons-and-planes/2015/11/grime-hip-hop|archive-date=14 September 2019|url-status=live}}{{Cite web|url=https://theconversation.com/skepta-grime-and-urban-british-youth-language-a-guide-65611|title=Skepta, grime and urban British youth language: a guide|website=The Conversation|date=21 September 2016 |url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191008174156/http://theconversation.com/skepta-grime-and-urban-british-youth-language-a-guide-65611|archive-date=8 October 2019}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/grime-is-approaching-the-breakthrough-moment-hip-hop-reached-in-the-90s/|title=Grime is Approaching the Breakthrough Moment Hip-Hop Reached in the 90s|date=21 December 2016|website=Vice|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191105013003/https://www.vice.com/en_uk/article/53gam8/grime-is-approaching-the-breakthrough-moment-hip-hop-reached-in-the-90s|archive-date=5 November 2019}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.standard.co.uk/go/london/music/grime-time-what-it-is-and-where-to-find-it-a3247511.html|title=Grime time: What it is and where to find it|date=13 May 2016|website=Standard|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191025044957/https://www.standard.co.uk/go/london/music/grime-time-what-it-is-and-where-to-find-it-a3247511.html|archive-date=25 October 2019}}{{Cite web|url=http://uk.complex.com/music/2016/06/hip-hop-dancehall-breaking-down-the-origins-of-grime/dizzee-talks-hip-hop-rosenberg|title=Hip-Hop Or Dancehall? Such success has caused a surge in media exposure of other British hip-hop acts. Welsh rap group [[Goldie Lookin Chain]] also achieved chart success with their tongue-in-cheek take on hip-hop. Key records such as [[Skinnyman]]'s ''[[Council Estate of Mind]]'', and [[Klashnekoff]]'s ''[[The Sagas Of...]]'' were released, cementing the reputations of the artists and opening up the floor for new artists to emerge. Labels [[Low Life Records]], run by prominent political rapper [[Braintax]], and Young N' Restless started and became the starting point for many.{{Cite web|url=https://djbooth.net/features/2019-04-09-london-hip-hop-new-york-in-1994-15-year-anniversary|title=London Hip-Hop's New York in '94: The 15-Year Anniversary|last=Oliver|first=M.|website=DJBooth|date=9 April 2019 |access-date=18 December 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191105153131/https://djbooth.net/features/2019-04-09-london-hip-hop-new-york-in-1994-15-year-anniversary|archive-date=5 November 2019|url-status=live}} At the same time, just as [[UK garage|garage]] was losing momentum, [[Grime (music genre)|grime]] was creating interest. [[Dizzee Rascal]] would release his debut studio album ''[[Boy in da Corner]]'' in 2003 to widespread critical acclaim and would go on to win the [[Mercury Prize]] and be certified Platinum by the [[British Phonographic Industry]] (BPI), while Wiley's ''[[Treddin' on Thin Ice]]'' (2004) became a cornerstone of the genre. From then on, grime artists were the only MC's for interested record labels, and UK Hip-Hop's momentum dried up.[[File:Skepta & P Diddy (& Chipmunk) Backstage at orange rock corps.png|thumb|280x280px|Chipmunk (left) and Skepta (right) with American rapper [[Sean Combs]] in 2011. Combs has also given recognition to Stormzy.{{Cite web|url=http://grmdaily.com/diddy-shouts-out-stormzy|title=Diddy shouts out Stormzy|website=GRM Daily – Grime, Rap music and Culture|date=10 June 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190510215716/http://grmdaily.com/diddy-shouts-out-stormzy|archive-date=10 May 2019|access-date=17 September 2019}}|alt=]]A new generation of young socially [[conscious hip-hop]] musicians emerged as a counter to the grime scene that many in the UK Hip-hop scene perceived as commercial. These rappers strived to bring attention to both positivity and lyricism as well as the injustices of war, gentrification and racism, following in the tradition of conscious rappers such as [[Nas]], [[Mos Def]] and [[Talib Kweli]]. Amongst this new generation included artists such as [[Klashnekoff]], [[Akala (rapper)|Akala]], [[Lowkey]] and the Poisonous Poets. The mid-2000s saw the emergence of [[road rap]], a genre that took influences from American gangsta rap and focused on crime, gang, or violent themes. Road rap was pioneered by artists and groups such as [[PDC (rap group)|PDC]] and [[Giggs (rapper)|Giggs]]' SN1 crew.{{Cite web|url=https://pitchfork.com/features/grime-dubstep/7901-grime-dubstep/|title=Grime / Dubstep|website=Pitchfork|date=17 November 2010 |access-date=18 December 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190424054128/https://pitchfork.com/features/grime-dubstep/7901-grime-dubstep/|archive-date=24 April 2019|url-status=live}} By the late 2000s, [[Grime (music genre)|grime music]] had entered into a period of stagnation.{{Cite web|url=https://www.anothermanmag.com/life-culture/10370/a-brief-history-of-grime-as-told-by-dj-target|title=A Brief History of Grime, as Told by DJ Target|last=AnotherMan|website=AnotherMan|date=12 June 2018 |access-date=13 September 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190913222453/https://www.anothermanmag.com/life-culture/10370/a-brief-history-of-grime-as-told-by-dj-target|archive-date=13 September 2019|url-status=live}}{{Cite news|url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2018/10/01/the-surprising-survival-of-grime|title=The Surprising Survival of Grime|last=Hsu|first=Hua|magazine=The New Yorker|date=24 September 2018|access-date=13 September 2019|issn=0028-792X|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190909050605/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2018/10/01/the-surprising-survival-of-grime|archive-date=9 September 2019|url-status=live}} This led to an emergence of acts that, while influenced by or initially started out making grime, were moving into a more commercialised, hip-hop influenced form of music. Artists from this new wave included [[N-Dubz]], [[Tinchy Stryder]], [[Tinie Tempah]], and [[Chipmunk (rapper)|Chipmunk]] (later known as Chip) who emerged in the late 2000s to great commercial success. Tinchy Stryder scored two number ones with songs "[[Number 1 (Tinchy Stryder song)|Number 1]]" and "[[Never Leave You]]" and became the best-selling British solo artist of 2009.{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/music/reviews/fmq4/ |title=Music – Review of Tinchy Stryder – Catch 22 |publisher=BBC |date=17 August 2009 |access-date=24 February 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160109182218/http://www.bbc.co.uk/music/reviews/fmq4 |archive-date=9 January 2016 |url-status=live }} The following year continued the success of the previous, with acts like [[Professor Green]] and [[Tinie Tempah]] breaking through to even bigger commercial success and also critical appreciation. UK rap, also known as British hip-hop or UK hip-hop or British rap, is a music genre and culture that covers a variety of styles of hip-hop made in the United Kingdom. The development of UK rap was shaped by a distinct set of regional influences, slang, and grassroots movements that differentiated it from American hip-hop.
It is generally classified as one of a number of styles of R&B/hip-hop. 
British hip-hop can also be referred to as Brit-hop, a term coined and popularised mainly by British Vogue magazine and the BBC. British hip-hop was originally influenced by the dub/toasting introduced to the United Kingdom by Jamaican migrants in the 1950s–70s, who eventually developed uniquely influenced rapping (or speed-toasting) to match the rhythm of the ever-increasing pace and aggression of Jamaican-influenced dub in the UK. 
Toasting and soundsystem cultures were also influential in genres outside of hip-hop that still included rapping – such as grime, jungle, and UK garage.
In 2003, The Times described British hip-hop's broad-ranging approach:

..."UK hip-hop" is a broad sonic church, encompassing anything made in Britain by musicians informed or inspired by hip-hop's possibilities, whose music is a response to the same stimuli that gave birth to rap in New York in the mid-Seventies.Although the underground scene was well established by the late 1980s, UK rap music saw little commercial success for several decades. Outside of a few exceptions such as Derek B and later the birth of trip-hop, from the 1980s until the early 2010s UK rap made up a small percentage of album sales in the domestic market. Performers saw wider success in the 2020s, including Stormzy headlining Glastonbury Festival, Dave releasing back-to-back UK number one albums with Psychodrama followed by We're All Alone in This Together, and Little Simz winning the Mercury Prize.
